Across three independent enrichment paradigms — RaMP multi-DB ORA (FDR 1.34e-13), Mummichog m/z-network activity (p=0.000252), and MetaboAnalystR KEGG PSEA (p=8.39e-06) — the Androgen and Estrogen Metabolism pathway emerges as the unambiguous top hit. These five metabolites hit the same biological module in RaMP (SMPDB:SMP00068, KEGG:map00150), mapped to the KEGG:hsa00140 namespace in MetaboAnalystR, and resolved with 100% overlap in the Mummichog KEGG network module. Spermidine and S-adenosylhomocysteine contributed a secondary signal in the urea cycle/amino group metabolism (Mummichog, p=0.033) and biological oxidations (RaMP), consistent with polyamine biosynthesis and methyl-donor cycling. Tetrahydrobiopterin appeared in biopterin and tyrosine metabolism but without statistical significance. The convergent steroid signal suggests the treatment perturbs the CYP17A1/ aromatase axis or steroid sulfatase activity — enzymes central to inter-conversion of DHEA, androstenedione, testosterone, and estrogens. This pattern is characteristic of altered sex steroid homeostasis, consistent with endocrine modulation, hormone replacement, or steroidogenesis inhibition.

Five C18/C19/C21 steroids drove the signal: testosterone, 17β-estradiol, estrone, 5α-dihydrotestosterone, and dehydroepiandrosterone. These five metabolites hit the same biological module in RaMP (SMPDB:SMP00068, KEGG:map00150), mapped to the KEGG:hsa00140 namespace in MetaboAnalystR, and resolved with 100% overlap in the Mummichog KEGG network module. Spermidine and S-adenosylhomocysteine contributed a secondary signal in the urea cycle/amino group metabolism (Mummichog, p=0.033) and biological oxidations (RaMP), consistent with polyamine biosynthesis and methyl-donor cycling. Tetrahydrobiopterin appeared in biopterin and tyrosine metabolism but without statistical significance. The convergent steroid signal suggests the treatment perturbs the CYP17A1/ aromatase axis or steroid sulfatase activity — enzymes central to inter-conversion of DHEA, androstenedione, testosterone, and estrogens. This pattern is characteristic of altered sex steroid homeostasis, consistent with endocrine modulation, hormone replacement, or steroidogenesis inhibition.
